id="Name">Name</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Name">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Etymology">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg/220px-DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg" width="220" height="293" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg/330px-DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg/440px-DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1536" data-file-height="2048" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:DSC00426_-_Statua_cineraria_etrusca_-_Proserpina-defunta_con_melagrana-_Foto_G._Dall%27Orto.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Persephone or &quot;the deceased woman&quot; holding a <A href="/wiki/Pomegranate" title="Pomegranate">pomegranate</A>. Etruscan terracotta cinerary statue. National archaeological museum in <A href="/wiki/Palermo" title="Palermo">Palermo</A>, Italy</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>In a <A href="/wiki/Linear_B" title="Linear B">Linear B</A> (<A href="/wiki/Mycenean_Greek" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenean Greek">Mycenean Greek</A>) inscription on a tablet found at <A href="/wiki/Pylos" title="Pylos">Pylos</A> dated 1400–1200 BC, <A href="/wiki/John_Chadwick" title="John Chadwick">John Chadwick</A> reconstructed<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[n 1]</A></SUP> the name of a goddess <I>*Preswa</I> who could be identified with <A href="/wiki/Oceanid" title="Oceanid">Persa</A>, daughter of <A href="/wiki/Oceanus" title="Oceanus">Oceanus</A> and found speculative the further identification with the first element of Persephone.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[4]</A></SUP> <SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[5]</A></SUP> <I>Persephonē</I> (<A href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</A>: <SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Περσεφόνη</SPAN>) is her name in the <A href="/wiki/Ionic_Greek" title="Ionic Greek">Ionic Greek</A> of <A href="/wiki/Epic_poetry" title="Epic poetry">epic</A> literature. The Homeric form of her name is <I>Persephoneia</I> (Περσεφονεία,<SUP id="cite_ref-Homer1899_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Homer1899-7">[6]</A></SUP> <I>Persephoneia</I>). In other dialects, she was known under variant names: <I>Persephassa</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Περσεφάσσα</SPAN>), <I>Persephatta</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Περσεφάττα</SPAN>), or simply <I>Korē</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Κόρη</SPAN>, &quot;girl, maiden&quot;).<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[7]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Plato" title="Plato">Plato</A> calls her <I>Pherepapha</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Φερέπαφα</SPAN>) in his <A href="/wiki/Cratylus_(dialogue)" title="Cratylus (dialogue)"><I>Cratylus</I></A>, &quot;because she is wise and touches that which is in motion&quot;. There are also the forms <I>Periphona</I> (Πηριφόνα) and <I>Phersephassa</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Φερσέφασσα</SPAN>). The existence of so many different forms shows how difficult it was for the Greeks to pronounce the word in their own language and suggests that the name may have a <A href="/wiki/Pre-Greek" class="mw-redirect" title="Pre-Greek">Pre-Greek</A> origin.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[8]</A></SUP>\n</P><P><I>Persephatta</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Περσεφάττα</SPAN>) is considered to mean &quot;female thresher of grain&quot;; the first constituent of the name originates in <A href="/wiki/Proto-Greek" class="mw-redirect" title="Proto-Greek">Proto-Greek</A> &quot;perso-&quot; (related to Sanskrit &quot;parṣa-&quot;), &quot;sheaf of grain&quot; and the second constituent of the name originates in Proto-Indo European <I><SPAN title="Proto-Indo-European language" class="Unicode" lang="ine" style="white-space:nowrap;">*-gʷn-t-ih</SPAN></I>, from the root <I><SPAN title="Proto-Indo-European language" class="Unicode" lang="ine" style="white-space:nowrap;">*gʷʰen-</SPAN></I> &quot;to strike&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[9]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>An alternative etymology is from <SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">φέρειν φόνον</SPAN>, <I>pherein phonon</I>, &quot;to bring (or cause) death&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-SmithPersephone_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SmithPersephone-11">[10]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Roman_Proserpina">Roman Proserpina</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Roman Proserpina">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg/220px-Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg" width="220" height="294" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg/330px-Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg/440px-Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1700" data-file-height="2270" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Proserpina_kidnapped_Kircheriano_Terme.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Cinerary altar with tabula representing the rape of <A href="/wiki/Proserpina" title="Proserpina">Proserpina</A>. White marble, Antonine Era, 2nd century <A href="/wiki/Rome" title="Rome">Rome</A>, Baths of Diocletian</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg/220px-Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg" width="220" height="238" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg/330px-Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg/440px-Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1080" data-file-height="1170" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Locri_Pinax_Persephone_Opens_Liknon_Mystikon.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Persephone opening a <I><A href="/wiki/Cista" title="Cista">cista</A></I> containing the infant <A href="/wiki/Adonis" title="Adonis">Adonis</A>, on a <A href="/wiki/Pinax" title="Pinax">pinax</A> from <A href="/wiki/Locri" title="Locri">Locri</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>The <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Romans</A> first heard of her from the <A href="/wiki/Aeolians" title="Aeolians">Aeolian</A> and <A href="/wiki/Dorians" title="Dorians">Dorian</A> cities of <A href="/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia">Magna Graecia</A>, who used the dialectal variant <I>Proserpinē</I> (<SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Προσερπίνη</SPAN>). Hence, in <A href="/wiki/Roman_mythology" title="Roman mythology">Roman mythology</A> she was called <A href="/wiki/Proserpina" title="Proserpina">Proserpina</A>, a name erroneously derived by the Romans from <I>proserpere</I>, &quot;to shoot forth&quot;<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[11]</A></SUP> and as such became an emblematic figure of the <A href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[12]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>At <A href="/wiki/Locri" title="Locri">Locri</A>, perhaps uniquely, Persephone was the protector of marriage, a role usually assumed by <A href="/wiki/Hera" title="Hera">Hera</A>; in the iconography of <A href="/wiki/Pinax" title="Pinax">votive plaques</A> at Locri, her abduction and marriage to Hades served as an emblem of the marital state, children at Locri were dedicated to Proserpina, and maidens about to be wed brought their <I><A href="/wiki/Peplos" title="Peplos">peplos</A></I> to be blessed.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[13]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Nestis">Nestis</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Nestis">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<P>In a Classical period text ascribed to <A href="/wiki/Empedocles" title="Empedocles">Empedocles</A>, c. 490 – 430 BC,<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[n 2]</A></SUP> describing a correspondence among four deities and the <A href="/wiki/Classical_element" title="Classical element">classical elements</A>, the name <I>Nestis</I> for water apparently refers to Persephone: &quot;Now hear the fourfold roots of everything: enlivening Hera, Hades, shining Zeus. And Nestis, moistening mortal springs with tears.&quot;<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[14]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>Of the four deities of Empedocles&#39; elements, it is the name of Persephone alone that is <A href="/wiki/Taboo" title="Taboo">taboo</A>—Nestis is a euphemistic cult title<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[n 3]</A></SUP>—for she was also the terrible Queen of the Dead, whose name was not safe to speak aloud, who was <A href="/wiki/Euphemism" title="Euphemism">euphemistically</A> named simply as Kore or &quot;the Maiden&quot;, a vestige of her archaic role as the deity ruling the underworld.\n</P>\n<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Titles_and_functions">Titles and functions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: Titles and functions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>\n<P>The epithets of Persephone reveal her double function as <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> and vegetation goddess. The surnames given to her by the poets refer to her character as Queen of the lower world and the dead, or her symbolic meaning of the power that shoots forth and withdraws into the earth. Her common name as a vegetation goddess is Kore, and in <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A> she was worshipped under the title <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A>, &quot;the mistress&quot;, a very old chthonic divinity. <A href="/wiki/Plutarch" title="Plutarch">Plutarch</A> identifies her with spring and <A href="/wiki/Cicero" title="Cicero">Cicero</A> calls her the seed of the fruits of the fields. In the <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian">Eleusinian</A> mysteries, her return is the symbol of immortality and hence she was frequently represented on sarcophagi.<SUP id="cite_ref-SmithPersephone_11-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SmithPersephone-11">[10]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>In the mystical theories of the <A href="/wiki/Orphism_(religion)" title="Orphism (religion)">Orphics</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Plato" title="Plato">Platonists</A>, Kore is described as the all-pervading goddess of nature<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[15]</A></SUP> who both produces and destroys everything, and she is therefore mentioned along or identified with other mystic divinities such as <A href="/wiki/Isis" title="Isis">Isis</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rhea_(mythology)" title="Rhea (mythology)">Rhea</A>, <A href="/wiki/Gaia_(mythology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Gaia (mythology)">Ge</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hestia" title="Hestia">Hestia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pandora" title="Pandora">Pandora</A>, <A href="/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis">Artemis</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Hecate" title="Hecate">Hecate</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[16]</A></SUP> The Orphic Persephone is further said to have become by <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A> the mother of <A href="/wiki/Dionysus" title="Dionysus">Dionysus</A>, <A href="/wiki/Iacchus" title="Iacchus">Iacchus</A>, <A href="/wiki/Zagreus" title="Zagreus">Zagreus</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-SmithPersephone_11-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SmithPersephone-11">[10]</A></SUP> and the little-attested <A href="/wiki/Melinoe" class="mw-redirect" title="Melinoe">Melinoe</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[17]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Epithets">Epithets</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Epithets">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<P>As a goddess of the underworld, Persephone was given <A href="/wiki/Euphemistically" class="mw-redirect" title="Euphemistically">euphemistically</A> friendly names.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP> However it is possible that some of them were the names of original goddesses:\n</P>\n<UL><LI><B><A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A></B> (<I>dems-potnia</I>) &quot;the mistress&quot; (literally &quot;the mistress of the house&quot;) in <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>Hagne</B>, &quot;pure&quot;, originally a goddess of the springs in <A href="/wiki/Messenia" title="Messenia">Messenia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-auto_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-auto-22">[19]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B>Melindia</B> or <B>Melinoia</B> (meli, &quot;honey&quot;), as the consort of <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A>, in Hermione. (Compare <A href="/wiki/Hecate" title="Hecate">Hecate</A>, <A href="/wiki/Melinoe" class="mw-redirect" title="Melinoe">Melinoe</A>)<SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B>Melivia</B><SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B>Melitodes</B><SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B>Aristi cthonia</B>, &quot;the best <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A>&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B><A href="/wiki/Praxidike" title="Praxidike">Praxidike</A></B>, the <A href="/wiki/Orphic" class="mw-redirect" title="Orphic">Orphic</A> Hymn to Persephone identifies Praxidike as an <A href="/wiki/Epithet" title="Epithet">epithet</A> of Persephone: &quot;Praxidike, subterranean queen. The <A href="/wiki/Erinyes" title="Erinyes">Eumenides</A>&#39; source [mother], fair-haired, whose frame proceeds from Zeus&#39; ineffable and secret seeds.&quot;<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[20]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[21]</A></SUP></LI></UL>\n<P>As a vegetation goddess, she was called:<SUP id="cite_ref-auto_22-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-auto-22">[19]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson463_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson463-25">[22]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<UL><LI><B>Kore</B>, &quot;the maiden&quot;.</LI>\n<LI><B>Kore Soteira</B>, &quot;the savior maiden&quot;, in <A href="/wiki/Megalopolis,_Greece" title="Megalopolis, Greece">Megalopolis</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>Neotera</B>, &quot;the younger&quot;, in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>Kore of Demeter Hagne</B> in the <A href="/wiki/Homeric_hymn" class="mw-redirect" title="Homeric hymn">Homeric hymn</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>Kore memagmeni</B>, &quot;the mixed daughter&quot; (bread).</LI></UL>\n<P><A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> and her daughter <B>Persephone</B> were usually called:<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson463_25-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson463-25">[22]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson478_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson478-26">[23]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<UL><LI><B>The goddesses</B>, often distinguished as &quot;the older&quot; and &quot;the younger&quot; in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>Demeters</B>, in <A href="/wiki/Rhodes" title="Rhodes">Rhodes</A> and <A href="/wiki/Sparta" title="Sparta">Sparta</A></LI>\n<LI><B>The thesmophoroi</B>, &quot;the legislators&quot; in the <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>The Great Goddesses</B>, in <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A>.</LI>\n<LI><B>The mistresses</B> in <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Pausanias515_27-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Pausanias515-27">[24]</A></SUP></LI>\n<LI><B>Karpophoroi</B>, &quot;the bringers of fruit&quot;, in <A href="/wiki/Tegea" title="Tegea">Tegea</A> of Arcadia.</LI></UL>\n<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Origins_of_the_cult">Origins of the cult</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: Origins of the cult">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:P1010629_crop.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/P1010629_crop.png/220px-P1010629_crop.png" width="220" height="173" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/P1010629_crop.png/330px-P1010629_crop.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/P1010629_crop.png/440px-P1010629_crop.png 2x" data-file-width="467" data-file-height="368" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:P1010629_crop.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Gold ring from Isopata tomb, near <A href="/wiki/Knossos" title="Knossos">Knossos</A>, <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, 1400–1500 BC. Depicted are female figures dancing among blossoming vegetation; <A href="/wiki/Heraklion_Archaeological_Museum" title="Heraklion Archaeological Museum">Heraklion Archaeological Museum</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>The myth of <A href="/wiki/Rape_of_Persephone" title="Rape of Persephone">a goddess being abducted and taken to the Underworld</A> is probably <A href="/wiki/Pre-Greek_substrate" title="Pre-Greek substrate">Pre-Greek</A> in origin. <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Noah_Kramer" title="Samuel Noah Kramer">Samuel Noah Kramer</A>, the renowned scholar of ancient <A href="/wiki/Sumer" title="Sumer">Sumer</A>, has posited that the Greek story of the abduction of Persephone may be derived from an ancient Sumerian story in which <A href="/wiki/Ereshkigal" title="Ereshkigal">Ereshkigal</A>, the ancient Sumerian goddess of the Underworld, is abducted by <A href="/wiki/Kur" class="mw-redirect" title="Kur">Kur</A>, the primeval <A href="/wiki/Dragon" title="Dragon">dragon</A> of <A href="/wiki/Sumerian_religion" title="Sumerian religion">Sumerian mythology</A>, and forced to become ruler of the Underworld against her own will.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[25]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The location of Persephone&#39;s abduction is different in each local cult. The <I><A href="/wiki/Homeric_Hymns" title="Homeric Hymns">Homeric Hymn to Demeter</A></I> mentions the &quot;plain of Nysa&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[26]</A></SUP> The locations of this probably mythical place may simply be conventions to show that a magically distant <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> land of myth was intended in the remote past.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[27]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Sherwood217_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sherwood217-31">[28]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> found and met her daughter in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>, and this is the mythical disguise of what happened in the mysteries.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert285_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert285-32">[29]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>Persephone is an old <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> deity of the agricultural communities, who received the souls of the dead into the earth, and acquired powers over the fertility of the soil, over which she reigned. The earliest depiction of a goddess who may be identified with Persephone growing out of the ground, is on a plate from the Old-Palace period in <A href="/wiki/Phaistos" title="Phaistos">Phaistos</A>. The goddess has a vegetable-like appearance, and she is surrounded by dancing girls between blossoming flowers.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert42_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert42-33">[30]</A></SUP>  A similar representation, where the goddess appears to come down from the sky, is depicted on the <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> ring of Isopata.\n</P>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg/220px-Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg" width="220" height="200" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg/330px-Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg/440px-Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2124" data-file-height="1935" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Persephone_krater_Antikensammlung_Berlin_1984.40.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Rape_of_Persephone" title="Rape of Persephone">Rape of Persephone</A>. <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> with his horses and <B>Persephone</B> (down). An Apulian red-figure volute krater, c. 340 BC. <A href="/wiki/Antikensammlung_Berlin" title="Antikensammlung Berlin">Antikensammlung Berlin</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>In some forms <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> appears with his <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> horses. The myth of the rape of Kore was derived from the idea that <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> catches the souls of the dead and then carries them with his horses into his kingdom. This idea is vague in <A href="/wiki/Homer" title="Homer">Homer</A>, but appears in later Greek depictions, and in Greek folklore. &quot;Charos&quot; appears with his horse and carries the dead into the underworld.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Charon_35-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Charon-35">[32]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The cults of Persephone and <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian mysteries">Eleusinian mysteries</A> and in the <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A> were based on old agrarian cults.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[33]</A></SUP>\nA lot of ancient beliefs were based on initiation into jealously-guarded <A href="/wiki/Mystery_religions" class="mw-redirect" title="Mystery religions">mysteries</A> (secret rites) because they offered prospects after death more enjoyable than the final end at the gloomy space of the Greek <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A>. There is evidence that some practices were derived from the religious practices of the <A href="/wiki/Mycenean_Greece" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenean Greece">Mycenaean age</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Dietrich220_37-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Dietrich220-37">[34]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert42_33-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert42-33">[30]</A></SUP>  <A href="/wiki/Karl_Kerenyi" class="mw-redirect" title="Karl Kerenyi">Kerenyi</A> asserts that these religious practices were introduced from <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>.,<SUP id="cite_ref-Kerenyi24_38-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kerenyi24-38">[35]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Kerenyi31_39-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kerenyi31-39">[36]</A></SUP> The idea of immortality which appears in the syncretistic religions of the <A href="/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East">Near East</A> did not exist in the Eleusinian mysteries at the very beginning.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[37]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[38]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Near_East_and_Minoan_Crete">Near East and Minoan Crete</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: Near East and Minoan Crete">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg/220px-Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg" width="220" height="333" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg/330px-Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg/440px-Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="3333" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Lady_of_Auxerre_Louvre_Ma3098_n2.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Lady_of_Auxerre" title="Lady of Auxerre">Lady of Auxerre</A> <A href="/wiki/Louvre" title="Louvre">Louvre</A>-An Archaic (640 BC) image from <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>. A version of a Minoan goddess who may be identified with Kore</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>In the <A href="/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East">Near eastern</A> myth of the early agricultural societies, every year the fertility goddess bore the &quot;god of the new year&quot;, who then became her lover, and died immediately in order to be reborn and face the same destiny. Some findings from <A href="/wiki/Catal_Huyuk" class="mw-redirect" title="Catal Huyuk">Catal Huyuk</A> since the Neolithic age,  indicate the worship of the Great Goddess  accompanied by a boyish consort, who symbolizes the annual  decay and return of vegetation.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[39]</A></SUP> Similar cults of resurrected gods appear in the Near East and <A href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</A> in the cults of <A href="/wiki/Attis" title="Attis">Attis</A>, <A href="/wiki/Adonis" title="Adonis">Adonis</A> and <A href="/wiki/Osiris" title="Osiris">Osiris</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[40]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>In <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, the &quot;divine child&quot; was related to the female vegetation divinity <A href="/wiki/Ariadne" title="Ariadne">Ariadne</A> who died every year.<SUP id="cite_ref-Schacherm141_44-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Schacherm141-44">[41]</A></SUP>  The <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> religion had its own characteristics. The most peculiar feature of the Minoan belief in the divine, is the appearance of the goddess from above in the dance. Dance floors have been discovered in addition to &quot;vaulted tombs&quot;, and it seems that the dance was ecstatic. <A href="/wiki/Homer" title="Homer">Homer</A> memorializes the dance floor which <A href="/wiki/Daedalus" title="Daedalus">Daedalus</A> built for <A href="/wiki/Ariadne" title="Ariadne">Ariadne</A> in the remote past.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert34_45-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert34-45">[42]</A></SUP> On the gold ring from Isopata, four women in festal attire are performing a dance between blossoming flowers. Above a figure apparently floating in the air seems to be the goddess herself, appearing amid the whirling dance.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert40_46-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert40-46">[43]</A></SUP> An image plate from the first palace of <A href="/wiki/Phaistos" title="Phaistos">Phaistos</A>, seems to be very close to the mythical image of the <I>Anodos</I> (ascent) of Persephone. Two girls dance between blossoming flowers, on each side of a similar but armless and legless figure which seems to grow out of the ground. The goddess is bordered by snake lines which give her a vegetable like appearance  She has a large stylized flower turned over her head. The resemblance with the flower-picking Persephone and her companions is compelling.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert42_33-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert42-33">[30]</A></SUP> The depiction of the goddess is similar to later images of &quot;Anodos of Pherephata&quot;. On the Dresden vase, Persephone is growing out of the ground, and she is surrounded by the animal-tailed agricultural gods <A href="/wiki/Seilenos" class="mw-redirect" title="Seilenos">Silenoi</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Hermesthe_47-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hermesthe-47">[44]</A></SUP>\n</P><P><A href="/wiki/Karl_Kerenyi" class="mw-redirect" title="Karl Kerenyi">Kerenyi</A> suggests that the name <A href="/wiki/Ariadne" title="Ariadne">Ariadne</A> (derived from <SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">ἁγνή</SPAN>, <I>hagne</I>, &quot;pure&quot;), was an <A href="/wiki/Euphemistical" class="mw-redirect" title="Euphemistical">euphemistical</A> name given by the Greeks to the nameless &quot;Mistress of the <A href="/wiki/Labyrinth" title="Labyrinth">labyrinth</A>&quot; who appears in a <A href="/wiki/Mycenean_Greece" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenean Greece">Mycenean Greek</A> inscription from <A href="/wiki/Knossos" title="Knossos">Knossos</A> in <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>. The Greeks used to give friendly names to the deities of the underworld. <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Cthonic Zeus</A> was called <A href="/wiki/Eubuleus" title="Eubuleus">Eubuleus</A>, &quot;the good counselor&quot;, and the ferryman of the river of the underworld <A href="/wiki/Charon_(mythology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Charon (mythology)">Charon</A>, &quot;glad&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-Charon_35-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Charon-35">[32]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A> and &quot;Hagne&quot; were probably euphemistic surnames of Persephone, therefore he theorizes that the cult of Persephone was the continuation of the worship of a <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> Great goddess. The <A href="/wiki/Labyrinth" title="Labyrinth">labyrinth</A> was both a winding dance-ground and, in the Greek view, a prison with the dreaded <A href="/wiki/Minotaur" title="Minotaur">Minotaur</A> at its centre.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[45]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[46]</A></SUP> It is possible that some religious practices, especially the <A href="/wiki/Mystery_religions" class="mw-redirect" title="Mystery religions">mysteries</A>, were transferred from a <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Cretan</A> priesthood to <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>, where <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> brought the <A href="/wiki/Poppy" title="Poppy">poppy</A> from <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[47]</A></SUP> Besides these similarities, <A href="/wiki/Walter_Burkert" title="Walter Burkert">Burkert</A> explains that up to now it is not known to what extent one can and must differentiate between <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mycenea" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenea">Mycenean</A> religion.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[48]</A></SUP> In the <A href="/wiki/Anthesteria" title="Anthesteria">Anthesteria</A> Dionysos is the &quot;divine child&quot;.\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Mycenean_Greece">Mycenean Greece</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: Mycenean Greece">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Fresco_of_two_female_charioteers_from_Tiryns_1200_BC.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Fresco_of_two_female_charioteers_from_Tiryns_1200_BC.jpg/220px-Fresco_of_two_female_charioteers_from_Tiryns_1200_BC.jpg" width="220" height="303" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2f/Fresco_of_two_female_charioteers_from_Tiryns_1200_BC.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="258" data-file-height="355" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Fresco_of_two_female_charioteers_from_Tiryns_1200_BC.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Two women or goddesses on a chariot. Fresco from <A href="/wiki/Tiryns" title="Tiryns">Tiryns</A>, 1200 BC. National Archaeological Museum of <A href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</A>.</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>There is evidence of a cult in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A> from the Mycenean period;<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[49]</A></SUP> however, there are not sacral finds from this period. The cult was private and there is no information about it. As well as the names of some Greek gods in the <A href="/wiki/Mycenean_Greece" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenean Greece">Mycenean Greek</A> inscriptions, also appear names of goddesses, like &quot;the divine Mother&quot; (the mother of the gods) or &quot;the Goddess (or priestess) of the winds&quot;, who don&#39;t have Mycenean origin .<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert285_32-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert285-32">[29]</A></SUP> In historical times, <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> and Kore were usually referred to as &quot;the goddesses&quot; or &quot;the mistresses&quot; (<A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A>) in the mysteries .<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[50]</A></SUP> In the <A href="/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece" title="Mycenaean Greece">Mycenean Greek</A> tablets dated 1400–1200 BC, the &quot;two queens and the king&quot; are mentioned. <A href="/wiki/John_Chadwick" title="John Chadwick">John Chadwick</A> believes that these were the precursor divinities of <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A>, Persephone and <A href="/wiki/Poseidon" title="Poseidon">Poseidon</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[51]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[52]</A></SUP> \n</P><P>Some information can be obtained from the study of the cult of <A href="/wiki/Eileithyia" title="Eileithyia">Eileithyia</A> at <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, and the cult of <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A>. In the cave of <A href="/wiki/Amnisos" title="Amnisos">Amnisos</A> at <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, <A href="/wiki/Eileithyia" title="Eileithyia">Eileithyia</A> is related with the annual birth of the divine child and she is connected with  <I>Enesidaon</I> (The earth shaker), who is the <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> aspect of the god <A href="/wiki/Poseidon" title="Poseidon">Poseidon</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Dietrich_p._220,221_56-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Dietrich_p._220,221-56">[53]</A></SUP> \nPersephone was conflated with Despoina, &quot;the mistress&quot;, a chthonic divinity in West-<A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Kerenyi31_39-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kerenyi31-39">[36]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Megaron" title="Megaron">megaron</A> of Eleusis is quite similar with the &quot;megaron&quot; of Despoina at <A href="/wiki/Lycosura" title="Lycosura">Lycosura</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert285_32-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert285-32">[29]</A></SUP> Demeter is united with the god <A href="/wiki/Poseidon" title="Poseidon">Poseidon</A>, and she bears a daughter, the unnameable Despoina.<SUP id="cite_ref-Pausanias_8.37.9_57-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Pausanias_8.37.9-57">[54]</A></SUP> Poseidon appears as a horse, as it usually happens in Northern European folklore. The goddess of nature and her companion survived in the Eleusinian cult, where the following words were uttered &quot;Mighty Potnia bore a great sun&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-Dietrich_p._220,221_56-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Dietrich_p._220,221-56">[53]</A></SUP> In Eleusis, in a ritual, one child (&quot;pais&quot;) was initiated from the hearth. The name <I>pais</I> (the divine child) appears in the Mycenean inscriptions,<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert285_32-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert285-32">[29]</A></SUP> and the ritual indicates the transition from the old funerary practices to the <A href="/wiki/Greece" title="Greece">Greek</A> cremation.<SUP id="cite_ref-Wunderlich_1972_p._134_58-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Wunderlich_1972_p._134-58">[55]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>In Greek mythology Nysa is a mythical mountain with an unknown location.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sherwood217_31-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sherwood217-31">[28]</A></SUP> <I>Nysion</I> (or Mysion), the place of the abduction of Persephone was also probably a mythical place which did not exist on the map, a magically distant chthonic land of myth which was intended in the remote past.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[56]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Mythology">Mythology</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=10" title="Edit section: Mythology">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Abduction_myth">Abduction myth</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=11" title="Edit section: Abduction myth">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_(detail).JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG/220px-Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG" width="220" height="126" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG/330px-Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG/440px-Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_%28detail%29.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3644" data-file-height="2084" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Sarcophagus_with_the_Abduction_of_Persephone_by_Hades_(detail).JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Sarcophagus" title="Sarcophagus">Sarcophagus</A> with the abduction of <B>Persephone</B>. Walters Art Museum. <A href="/wiki/Baltimore" title="Baltimore">Baltimore</A>, <A href="/wiki/Maryland" title="Maryland">Maryland</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>The story of her abduction by <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> against her will is traditionally referred to as the <A href="/wiki/Rape_of_Persephone" title="Rape of Persephone">Rape of Persephone</A>. It is mentioned briefly in <A href="/wiki/Hesiod" title="Hesiod">Hesiod</A>&#39;s <A href="/wiki/Theogony" title="Theogony">Theogony</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-HesTh914_60-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HesTh914-60">[57]</A></SUP> and told in considerable detail in the <I><A href="/wiki/Homeric_Hymns" title="Homeric Hymns">Homeric Hymn to Demeter</A></I>. Persephone used to live far away from the other gods, a goddess within Nature herself before the days of planting seeds and nurturing plants. In the Olympian telling, the gods <A href="/wiki/Hermes" title="Hermes">Hermes</A> and <A href="/wiki/Apollo" title="Apollo">Apollo</A> had wooed Persephone; but Demeter rejected all their gifts and hid her daughter away from the company of the Olympian gods.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[58]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A>, it is said, permitted <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A>, who was in love with the beautiful Persephone, to abduct her as her mother <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> was not likely to allow her daughter to go down to Hades. Persephone was gathering flowers with the <A href="/wiki/Oceanid" title="Oceanid">Oceanids</A> along with <A href="/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis">Artemis</A> and <A href="/wiki/Athena" title="Athena">Athena</A>—the <I>Homeric Hymn</I> says—in a field when <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> came to abduct her, bursting through a cleft in the earth.<SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[59]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A>, when she found her daughter had disappeared, searched for her all over the earth with Hecate&#39;s torches. In most versions she forbids the earth to produce, or she neglects the earth and in the depth of her despair she causes nothing to grow. <A href="/wiki/Helios" title="Helios">Helios</A>, the sun, who sees everything, eventually told Demeter what had happened and at length she discovered the place of her abode. Finally, Zeus, pressed by the cries of the hungry people and by the other deities who also heard their anguish, forced <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> to return Persephone.<SUP id="cite_ref-Theoi_Project_-_Persephone_63-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Theoi_Project_-_Persephone-63">[60]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg/220px-Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg" width="220" height="334" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg/330px-Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg/440px-Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4452" data-file-height="6768" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Rape_of_Prosepina_September_2015-3a.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/The_Rape_of_Proserpina" title="The Rape of Proserpina">The Rape of Proserpina</A> by <A href="/wiki/Gian_Lorenzo_Bernini" title="Gian Lorenzo Bernini">Gian Lorenzo Bernini</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Galleria_Borghese" title="Galleria Borghese">Galleria Borghese</A> in Rome.</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P><A href="/wiki/Hades_(mythology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Hades (mythology)">Hades</A> indeed complied with the request, but first he tricked her, giving her some <A href="/wiki/Pomegranate" title="Pomegranate">pomegranate</A> seeds to eat. Persephone was released by <A href="/wiki/Hermes" title="Hermes">Hermes</A>, who had been sent to retrieve her, but because she had tasted food in the underworld, she was obliged to spend a third of each year (the winter months) there, and the remaining part of the year with the gods above.<SUP id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-64">[61]</A></SUP> With the later writers Ovid and Hyginus, Persephone&#39;s time in the underworld becomes half the year.<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[62]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>Various local traditions place Persephone&#39;s abduction in a different location. The <A href="/wiki/Sicily" title="Sicily">Sicilians</A>, among whom her worship was probably introduced by the Corinthian and Megarian colonists, believed that Hades found her in the meadows near <A href="/wiki/Enna" title="Enna">Enna</A>, and that a well arose on the spot where he descended with her into the lower world. The <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Cretans</A> thought that their own island had been the scene of the rape, and the <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusinians</A> mentioned the Nysian plain in Boeotia, and said that Persephone had descended with Hades into the lower world at the entrance of the western <A href="/wiki/Oceanus" title="Oceanus">Oceanus</A>. Later accounts place the rape in <A href="/wiki/Attica" title="Attica">Attica</A>, near <A href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</A>, or near <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Theoi_Project_-_Persephone_63-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Theoi_Project_-_Persephone-63">[60]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_(1891).jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg/220px-Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg" width="220" height="291" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg/330px-Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg/440px-Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_%281891%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="773" data-file-height="1024" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Frederic_Leighton_-_The_Return_of_Persephone_(1891).jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><I>The return of Persephone</I>, by <A href="/wiki/Frederic_Leighton" title="Frederic Leighton">Frederic Leighton</A> (1891)</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>The <A href="/wiki/Homeric" class="mw-redirect" title="Homeric">Homeric</A> hymn mentions the <I>Nysion</I> (or Mysion) which was probably a mythical place. The location of this mythical place may simply be a convention to show that a magically distant <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> land of myth was intended in the remote past.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson463_25-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson463-25">[22]</A></SUP> Before Persephone was abducted by Hades, the shepherd Eumolpus and the swineherd <A href="/wiki/Eubuleus" title="Eubuleus">Eubuleus</A> saw a girl in a black chariot driven by an invisible driver being carried off into the earth which had violently opened up. Eubuleus was feeding his pigs at the opening to the underworld when Persephone was abducted by Plouton. His swine were swallowed by the earth along with her, and the myth is an etiology for the relation of pigs with the ancient rites in <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_66-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-66">[63]</A></SUP> and in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>.\n</P><P>In the hymn, Persephone returns and she is reunited with her mother near <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>. Demeter as she has been promised established her mysteries (orgies) when the Eleusinians built for her a temple near the spring of Callichorus. These were awful mysteries which were not allowed to be uttered. The uninitiated would spend a miserable existence in the gloomy space of <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> after death.<SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[n 4]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>In some versions, <A href="/wiki/Ascalaphus" title="Ascalaphus">Ascalaphus</A> informed the other deities that Persephone had eaten the pomegranate seeds. When Demeter and her daughter were reunited, the Earth flourished with vegetation and color, but for some months each year, when Persephone returned to the underworld, the earth once again became a barren realm. This is an <A href="/wiki/Origin_myth" title="Origin myth">origin story</A> to explain the seasons.\n</P><P>In an earlier version, <A href="/wiki/Hecate" title="Hecate">Hecate</A> rescued Persephone. On an Attic <A href="/wiki/Red-figure_pottery" title="Red-figure pottery">red-figured</A> <A href="/wiki/Krater" title="Krater">bell krater</A> of c. 440 BC in the <A href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art" title="Metropolitan Museum of Art">Metropolitan Museum of Art</A>, Persephone is rising as if up stairs from a cleft in the earth, while Hermes stands aside; Hecate, holding two torches, looks back as she leads her to the enthroned Demeter.<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[64]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The 10th-century <A href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine</A> encyclopedia <I><A href="/wiki/Suda" title="Suda">Suda</A></I> introduces a goddess of a blessed <A href="/wiki/Afterlife" title="Afterlife">afterlife</A> assured to <A href="/wiki/Orphism_(religion)" title="Orphism (religion)">Orphic mystery</A> initiates. This <A href="/wiki/Macaria" title="Macaria">Macaria</A> is asserted to be the daughter of Hades, but no mother is mentioned.<SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[65]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Interpretation_of_the_myth">Interpretation of the myth</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=12" title="Edit section: Interpretation of the myth">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg/220px-Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg" width="220" height="265" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg/330px-Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg/440px-Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg 2x" data-file-width="993" data-file-height="1198" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Locri_Pinax_Of_Persephone_And_Hades.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Pinax of Persephone and Hades from Locri. <A href="/wiki/Reggio_Calabria" title="Reggio Calabria">Reggio Calabria</A>, National Museum of Magna Graecia.</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>In the myth <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A> abducts Persephone to be his wife and the queen of his realm.<SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[66]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A> (Πλούτων, <I>Ploutōn</I>) was a name for the ruler of <A href="/wiki/Greek_underworld" title="Greek underworld">the underworld</A>; the god was also known as <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A>, a name for the underworld itself. The name <I>Pluton</I> was conflated with that of <A href="/wiki/Ploutos" class="mw-redirect" title="Ploutos">Ploutos</A> (Πλούτος <I>Ploutos</I>, &quot;wealth&quot;), a god of wealth, because mineral wealth was found underground, and because <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A> as a <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> god ruled the deep earth that contained the seeds necessary for a bountiful harvest.<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[67]</A></SUP> <I>Plouton</I> is lord of the dead, but as Persephone&#39;s husband he has serious claims to the powers of fertility.<SUP id="cite_ref-Athanas56_72-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Athanas56-72">[68]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>In the <A href="/wiki/Theogony" title="Theogony">Theogony</A> of <A href="/wiki/Hesiod" title="Hesiod">Hesiod</A>, <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> was united with the hero <A href="/wiki/Iasion" title="Iasion">Iasion</A> in <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A> and she bore <A href="/wiki/Ploutos" class="mw-redirect" title="Ploutos">Ploutos</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-HesTh914_60-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HesTh914-60">[57]</A></SUP> This union seems to be a reference to a <A href="/wiki/Hieros_gamos" title="Hieros gamos">hieros gamos</A> (ritual copulation) to ensure the earth&#39;s fertility.<SUP id="cite_ref-Athanas56_72-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Athanas56-72">[68]</A></SUP> This ritual copulation appears in <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, in many <A href="/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East">Near Eastern</A> agricultural societies, and also in the <A href="/wiki/Anthesteria" title="Anthesteria">Anthesteria</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[n 5]</A></SUP>\n</P><P><A href="/wiki/Martin_P._Nilsson" title="Martin P. Nilsson">Nilsson</A> believes that the original cult of <A href="/wiki/Ploutos" class="mw-redirect" title="Ploutos">Ploutos</A> (or <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A>) in <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A> was similar with the <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> cult of the &quot;divine child&quot;, who died in order to be reborn. The child was abandoned by his mother and then it was brought up by the powers of nature. Similar myths appear in the cults of <A href="/wiki/Hyakinthos" class="mw-redirect" title="Hyakinthos">Hyakinthos</A> (<A href="/wiki/Amyklai" class="mw-redirect" title="Amyklai">Amyklai</A>), <A href="/wiki/Erichthonios" class="mw-redirect" title="Erichthonios">Erichthonios</A> (<A href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</A>), and later in the cult of <A href="/wiki/Dionysos" class="mw-redirect" title="Dionysos">Dionysos</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-75">[70]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The Greek version of the abduction myth is related to grain\xa0–\xa0important and rare in the Greek environment\xa0–\xa0and the return (ascent) of Persephone was celebrated at the autumn sowing. <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A> (<A href="/wiki/Ploutos" class="mw-redirect" title="Ploutos">Ploutos</A>) represents the wealth of the grain that was stored in underground silos or ceramic jars (<I>pithoi</I>), during summer months. Similar subterranean <I>pithoi</I> were used in ancient times for burials and <A href="/wiki/Pluto_(mythology)" title="Pluto (mythology)">Pluto</A> is fused with <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A>, the King of the realm of the dead. During summer months, the Greek <I>grain-Maiden</I> (Kore) is lying in the grain of the underground silos in the realm of Hades, and she is fused with Persephone, the Queen of the Underworld. At the beginning of the autumn, when the seeds of the old crop are laid on the fields, she ascends and is reunited with her mother <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A>, for at that time the old crop and the new meet each other. For the initiated, this union was the symbol of the eternity of human life that flows from the generations which spring from each other.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilssonpopular51_76-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilssonpopular51-76">[71]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-77">[72]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Arcadian_myths">Arcadian myths</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=13" title="Edit section: Arcadian myths">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Lycosoura-group.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Lycosoura-group.jpg/220px-Lycosoura-group.jpg" width="220" height="68" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Lycosoura-group.jpg/330px-Lycosoura-group.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Lycosoura-group.jpg/440px-Lycosoura-group.jpg 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="246" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Lycosoura-group.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>From L-R, Artemis, Demeter, Veil of Despoina, Anytus, Tritoness from the throne of <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A> at <A href="/wiki/Lycosura" title="Lycosura">Lycosura</A>. <A href="/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Athens" class="mw-redirect" title="National Archaeological Museum of Athens">National Archaeological Museum of Athens</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P>The primitive myths of isolated <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadia</A> seem to be related to the first Greek-speaking people who came from the north-east during the <A href="/wiki/Bronze_age" class="mw-redirect" title="Bronze age">bronze age</A>. <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A> (the mistress), the goddess of the Arcadian mysteries, is the daughter of Demeter and <A href="/wiki/Poseidon" title="Poseidon">Poseidon</A> <I>Hippios</I> (horse), who represents the river spirit of the underworld that appears as a horse as often happens in northern-European folklore. He pursues the mare-Demeter and from the union she bears the horse <A href="/wiki/Arion_(mythology)" title="Arion (mythology)">Arion</A> and a daughter who originally had the form or the shape of a mare. The two goddesses were not clearly separated and they were closely connected with the springs and the animals. They were related with the god of rivers and springs; Poseidon and especially with <A href="/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis">Artemis</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Mistress_of_the_Animals" class="mw-redirect" title="Mistress of the Animals">Mistress of the Animals</A> who was the first <A href="/wiki/Nymph" title="Nymph">nymph</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson462_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson462-1">[1]</A></SUP> According to the Greek tradition a hunt-goddess preceded the harvest goddess.<SUP id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-78">[73]</A></SUP> In Arcadia, <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> and Persephone were often called <I>Despoinai</I> (Δέσποιναι, &quot;the mistresses&quot;) in historical times. They are the two Great Goddesses of the <A href="/wiki/Arcadia" title="Arcadia">Arcadian</A> cults, and evidently they come from a more primitive religion.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson463_25-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson463-25">[22]</A></SUP> The Greek god <A href="/wiki/Poseidon" title="Poseidon">Poseidon</A> probably substituted the companion (<I>Paredros</I>, Πάρεδρος) of the <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> <A href="/wiki/Mother_goddess" title="Mother goddess">Great goddess</A><SUP id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-79">[74]</A></SUP>\nin the Arcadian mysteries.\n</P>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Throning_goddess_(Persephone)_480-460_BC_(Sk_1761)_1.JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG/170px-Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG" width="170" height="256" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG/255px-Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG/340px-Throning_goddess_%28Persephone%29_480-460_BC_%28Sk_1761%29_1.JPG 2x" data-file-width="825" data-file-height="1243" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Throning_goddess_(Persephone)_480-460_BC_(Sk_1761)_1.JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Seated goddess, probably Persephone on her throne in the underworld, <A href="/wiki/Severe_style" title="Severe style">Severe style</A> <I>ca</I> 480–60, found at <A href="/wiki/Taranto" title="Taranto">Tarentum</A>, <A href="/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia">Magna Graecia</A> (<A href="/wiki/Pergamon_Museum" title="Pergamon Museum">Pergamon Museum</A>, Berlin)</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Queen_of_the_Underworld">Queen of the Underworld</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=14" title="Edit section: Queen of the Underworld">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<P>Persephone held an ancient role as the dread queen of the Underworld, within which tradition it was forbidden to speak her name. This tradition comes from her conflation with the very old <A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">chthonic</A> divinity <A href="/wiki/Despoina" title="Despoina">Despoina</A> (the mistress), whose real name could not be revealed to anyone except those initiated to her mysteries.<SUP id="cite_ref-Pausanias_8.37.9_57-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Pausanias_8.37.9-57">[54]</A></SUP> As goddess of death she was also called a daughter of <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A> and <A href="/wiki/Styx" title="Styx">Styx</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-80">[75]</A></SUP> the river that formed the boundary between <A href="/wiki/Earth" title="Earth">Earth</A> and the underworld. <A href="/wiki/Homer" title="Homer">Homer</A> describes her as the formidable, venerable majestic queen of the shades, who carries into effect the curses of men upon the souls of the dead, along with her husband Hades.<SUP id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-81">[76]</A></SUP> In the reformulation of Greek mythology expressed in the <I><A href="/wiki/Orphic_Hymns" class="mw-redirect" title="Orphic Hymns">Orphic Hymns</A></I>, Dionysus and Melinoe are separately called children of Zeus and Persephone.<SUP id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-82">[77]</A></SUP> Groves sacred to her stood at the western extremity of the earth on the frontiers of the lower world, which itself was called &quot;house of Persephone&quot;.<SUP id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-83">[78]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>Her central myth served as the context for the secret rites of regeneration at <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_Mysteries" title="Eleusinian Mysteries">Eleusis</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-84">[79]</A></SUP> which promised immortality to initiates.\n</P>\n<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cult_of_Persephone">Cult of Persephone</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=15" title="Edit section: Cult of Persephone">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>\n<P>Persephone was worshipped along with her mother <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> and in the same mysteries. Her cults included agrarian magic, dancing, and rituals. The priests used special vessels and holy symbols, and the people participated with rhymes. In <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A> there is evidence of sacred laws and other inscriptions.<SUP id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-85">[80]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The Cult of Demeter and the Maiden is found at <A href="/wiki/Attica" title="Attica">Attica</A>, in the main festivals <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A> and <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian mysteries">Eleusinian mysteries</A> and in a lot of local cults. These festivals were almost always celebrated at the autumn sowing, and at full-moon according to the Greek tradition. In some local cults the feasts were dedicated to Demeter.\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=16" title="Edit section: Thesmophoria">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A></DIV>\n<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Kore55.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kore55.jpg/220px-Kore55.jpg" width="220" height="293" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kore55.jpg/330px-Kore55.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kore55.jpg/440px-Kore55.jpg 2x" data-file-width="495" data-file-height="660" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Kore55.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Kore, daughter of Demeter, celebrated with her mother by the <A href="/wiki/Thesmophoriazusae" title="Thesmophoriazusae">Thesmophoriazusae</A> (women of the festival). <A href="/wiki/Acropolis_Museum" title="Acropolis Museum">Acropolis Museum</A>, Athens</DIV></DIV></DIV>\n<P><A href="/wiki/Thesmophoria" title="Thesmophoria">Thesmophoria</A>, were celebrated in <A href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</A>, and the festival was widely spread in Greece. This was a festival of secret women-only rituals connected with marriage customs and commemorated the third of the year, in the month <A href="/wiki/Attic_calendar" title="Attic calendar">Pyanepsion</A>, when Kore was abducted and Demeter abstained from her role as goddess of harvest and growth. The ceremony involved sinking sacrifices into the earth by night and retrieving the decaying remains of pigs that had been placed in the <I>megara</I> of Demeter (trenches and pits or natural clefts in rock), the previous year. These were placed on altars, mixed with seeds, then planted.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert240_86-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert240-86">[81]</A></SUP> Pits rich in organic matter at Eleusis have been taken as evidence that the Thesmophoria was held there as well as in other <A href="/wiki/Deme" title="Deme">demes</A> of <A href="/wiki/Attica" title="Attica">Attica</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-87">[82]</A></SUP> This agrarian magic was also used in the cult of the earth-goddesses <A href="/wiki/Potnia" title="Potnia">potniai</A> (mistresses) in the <A href="/wiki/Cabeiri" title="Cabeiri">Cabeirian</A>, and in <A href="/wiki/Knidos" title="Knidos">Knidos</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilsson151_88-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilsson151-88">[83]</A></SUP>\n</P><P>The festival was celebrated over three days. The first was the &quot;way up&quot; to the sacred space, the second, the day of feasting when they ate <A href="/wiki/Pomegranate" title="Pomegranate">pomegranate</A> seeds and the third was a meat feast in celebration of <A href="/wiki/Kalligeneia" class="mw-redirect" title="Kalligeneia">Kalligeneia</A> a goddess of beautiful birth. <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A> penetrated the mysteries as <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A>- <A href="/wiki/Eubuleus" title="Eubuleus">Eubuleus</A><SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert240_86-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert240-86">[81]</A></SUP> which is an <A href="/wiki/Euphemistically" class="mw-redirect" title="Euphemistically">euphemistical</A> name of <A href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</A> (<A href="/wiki/Chthonic" title="Chthonic">Chthonios</A> <A href="/wiki/Zeus" title="Zeus">Zeus</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-Rhode206_21-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rhode206-21">[18]</A></SUP> In the original myth which is an etiology for the ancient rites, Eubuleus was a swineherd who was feeding his pigs at the opening to the underworld when Persephone was abducted by Plouton. His swine were swallowed by the earth along with her.<SUP id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_66-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-66">[63]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Eleusinian_mysteries">Eleusinian mysteries</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Persephone&amp;action=edit&amp;section=17" title="Edit section: Eleusinian mysteries">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>\n<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian mysteries">Eleusinian mysteries</A></DIV>\n<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Eleusis2.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Eleusis2.jpg/170px-Eleusis2.jpg" width="170" height="245" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Eleusis2.jpg/255px-Eleusis2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Eleusis2.jpg/340px-Eleusis2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1308" data-file-height="1888" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Eleusis2.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>The <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian mysteries">Eleusinian trio</A>: Persephone, <A href="/wiki/Triptolemus" title="Triptolemus">Triptolemus</A> and <A href="/wiki/Demeter" title="Demeter">Demeter</A> on a marble bas-relief from <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>, 440–430 BC. <A href="/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Athens" class="mw-redirect" title="National Archaeological Museum of Athens">National Archaeological Museum of Athens</A></DIV></DIV></DIV> \n<P>The <A href="/wiki/Eleusinian_mysteries" class="mw-redirect" title="Eleusinian mysteries">Eleusinian mysteries</A> was a festival celebrated at the autumn sowing in the city of <A href="/wiki/Eleusis" title="Eleusis">Eleusis</A>. Inscriptions refer to &quot;the Goddesses&quot; accompanied by the agricultural god <A href="/wiki/Triptolemos" class="mw-redirect" title="Triptolemos">Triptolemos</A> (probably son of <A href="/wiki/Gaia_(mythology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Gaia (mythology)">Ge</A> and <A href="/wiki/Oceanus" title="Oceanus">Oceanus</A>),<SUP id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-89">[84]</A></SUP> and &quot;the God and the Goddess&quot; (Persephone and Plouton) accompanied by <A href="/wiki/Eubuleus" title="Eubuleus">Eubuleus</A> who probably led the way back from the underworld.<SUP id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-90">[85]</A></SUP> The myth was represented in a cycle with three phases: the &quot;descent&quot;, the &quot;search&quot;, and the &quot;ascent&quot;, with contrasted emotions from sorrow to joy which roused the mystae to exultation. The main theme was the ascent of Persephone and the reunion with her mother Demeter.<SUP id="cite_ref-Nilssonpopular51_76-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Nilssonpopular51-76">[71]</A></SUP> The festival activities included dancing, probably across the Rharian field, where according to the myth the first grain grew.\n</P><P>At the beginning of the feast, the priests filled two special vessels and poured them out, the one towards the west, and the other towards the east. The people looking both to the sky and the earth shouted in a magical rhyme &quot;rain and conceive&quot;. In a ritual, a child was initiated from the hearth (the divine fire). It was the ritual of the &quot;divine child&quot; who originally was <A href="/wiki/Ploutos" class="mw-redirect" title="Ploutos">Ploutos</A>. In the Homeric hymn the ritual is connected with the myth of the agricultural god <A href="/wiki/Triptolemos" class="mw-redirect" title="Triptolemos">Triptolemos</A><SUP id="cite_ref-Wunderlich_1972_p._134_58-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Wunderlich_1972_p._134-58">[55]</A></SUP> The high point of the celebration was &quot;an ear of grain cut in silence&quot;, which represented the force of the new life. The idea of immortality didn&#39;t exist in the mysteries at the beginning, but the initiated believed that they would have a better fate in the underworld. Death remained a reality, but at the same time a new beginning like the plant which grows from the buried seed.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert285_32-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert285-32">[29]</A></SUP> In the earliest depictions Persephone is an armless and legless deity, who grows out of the ground.<SUP id="cite_ref-Burkert42_33-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Burkert42-33">[30]</A></SUP>\n</P>\n<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Local_cults">Local cults</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A
